articles.title: Missing baby found alive buried in dog crate in South Carolina
articles.summary: An 11-month-old baby boy who officials said was taken by his father on Monday was found buried alive in a dog crate Tuesday, a discovery a South Carolina sheriff called “joyful.”
articles.body: An 11-month-old baby boy who officials said was taken by his father on Monday was found buried alive in a dog crate Tuesday, a discovery a South Carolina sheriff called “joyful.” Koah Sharpe was found alive in a dog crate wrapped in a towel, Lexington County Sheriff Bryan Koon told reporters. “That, by the grace of God, probably provided enough air for him to survive — our estimation is, for the last 24 hours under that dirt,” he said. Koah, described as a 20-pound boy with reddish hair and who had a pacifier, was taken by his father, Michael Comer, on Monday morning, the sheriff’s office said. The crate was found around 1:30 p.m. Tuesday, Koon said, near the home of Comer’s father. Comer was arrested late Monday in Lexington County on a burglary charge after he was found in an outbuilding. The baby was not with him, the sheriff’s office said. Koon said Comer’s mother was taking care of the baby Monday morning. Comer came over and his mother left, but another caregiver was on the way, the sheriff said. “By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone and Koah was gone with him,” he said. In a phone interview Tuesday with NBC News, Comer’s mother, Patricia Comer, said she was shocked and that her son being in police custody was “where he needs to be.” “Honestly, I’m his mother and I never expected this from him,” she said. Koah’s mother has full custody of the child, Patricia Comer said. But the boy’s mother would let Patricia Comer supervise him on weekends, and there was no custody agreement preventing Michael Comer from watching the child unsupervised, which he had done before with no problems, Patricia Comer said. She said she went to work Monday and left Koah in his father’s care. Then, at around 11 a.m., a friend went to the home to drop off some formula, but no one answered, prompting the friend to call her, Patricia Comer recalled. “Something just did not feel right. I told my boss, ‘I need to leave work,’” she said. “Call it mother’s instinct, I don’t know what it was.” She went home and “sure enough, Michael had left,” she said. The child was reported missing and law enforcement began a search. Deputies went to Comer’s father’s home Monday and found the doors open and baby belongings in the house but no sign of Comer or the child, Koon said. The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division, the FBI and federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives were part of the search for the child. A search party of nearly 100 police officers, firefighters and other officials looked for the boy, Koon said. Searchers on Tuesday found a site not far from Comer’s father’s house, about 50 yards into some woods with freshly disturbed earth, Koon said. “As they probed it and laid it out and started digging, you could hear little Koah crying,” the sheriff said. “So, as you can imagine, the race was on.” The baby was taken to a hospital, where he was being cared for Tuesday afternoon, Koon said. The sheriff said he hopes the child makes a full recovery. “He was screaming at the top of his lungs, which is a good thing in the baby world, I would guess,” Koon said. The wire crate, which was about 2 feet by 2 feet, was buried in a shallow hole, Koon said. Wrapping it in a towel probably created an air pocket, he said. Koon said authorities were working with the prosecutor’s office regarding charges. It was not immediately clear if Comer had an attorney who could speak on his behalf. Koon said the cool weather may also have helped the baby’s chances of survival. “A lot of things were going in Koah’s favor, and the good Lord looked down on him the last 24 hours,” he said. Patricia Comer said that what her son is accused of doing is “pure evil” and that there were no warning signs. She said her son lives with her after a recent jail stint in which he drunkenly went to the home of an ex of Koah’s mother. She added that “all he does is go to work and come home.” She also said she feels hurt that some people are blaming her. “Just know that if I could have prevented this, I would have done everything my power,” Patricia Comer said. “I had no idea this was going to happen.” She thanked the Lexington County Sheriff’s Office and all the agencies and officials who helped find her grandson alive. “I did not know he would do anything like this,” she said of her son. “He’s always been so good with Koah. Who would think their own child would do something like this?”

articles.title: An English couple paved a 1.4-metre wedge of their neighbour’s garden to widen access to a horse paddock in 2017; a tribunal has rejected their claim to the land, leaving the disputed driveway at risk
articles.summary: A long-running boundary dispute in Leicestershire has ended in a legal defeat for a couple who extended their driveway onto a neighbouring garden to
articles.body: A long-running boundary dispute in Leicestershire has ended in a legal defeat for a couple who extended their driveway onto a neighbouring garden to improve access to their horse paddock. Railway expert Dr Piers Connor and his partner, Professor Christine Pasquire, have failed to establish ownership of the disputed strip of land after a First-tier Tribunal rejected their claim under adverse possession laws. The case was reported by The Independent, The Telegraph and The Daily Mail on November 5, 2026. The disagreement involves a narrow, tapering section of land measuring up to 1.4 metres wide beside the neighbouring property in Kirby Bellars. Connor and Pasquire installed a block-paved accessway in 2017, intending to make it easier for larger vehicles to enter the paddock adjoining their home. Their neighbours, GP Dr Dawn Moore-Elphick and her husband Richard, objected to the development, arguing that the newly paved section encroached on their garden. By 2021, the disagreement had escalated, with the neighbours threatening to cut through and remove the portion of paving that extended onto their property.The couple’s claim to the disputed landConnor and Pasquire subsequently sought to establish ownership through adverse possession, a legal principle commonly associated with squatters’ rights. Under the rules governing registered land in England and Wales, applicants generally need to demonstrate at least 10 years of factual possession and an intention to possess the land.The couple argued that they had always understood the disputed accessway to belong to their property. They pointed to a large leylandii hedge that previously marked the edge of the neighbouring garden, saying they had regarded it as the boundary. They also argued that the area had been used by vehicles belonging to previous occupants of their home, with parts of the vehicles, including wing mirrors, regularly passing over the disputed section. An earlier covering of stones at the entrance was also presented as evidence of its historical use.However, the tribunal did not consider these activities sufficient to establish legal possession. It found that simply driving across another person’s land did not amount to taking control of it. Similarly, the earlier stone covering was not considered substantial enough to demonstrate factual possession.Why the tribunal rejected the applicationJudge Ewan Paton concluded that the couple’s qualifying possession of the disputed paved section began only in 2017, when contractors excavated the existing surface and installed the new driveway. This meant they had not completed the required 10-year period when their application was considered. The judge therefore directed the Chief Land Registrar to reject their request to have the disputed land registered in their names.The ruling also highlighted that the disagreement was fundamentally about access rather than ownership. The couple wanted a wider turning area to make it easier for vehicles to travel between their home and the paddock. The judge acknowledged that the narrow wedge was important to their preferred access arrangement. However, the tribunal heard no expert evidence establishing whether losing the section would make access impossible, more difficult or simply less convenient.Could the driveway have to be removed?The decision leaves the couple without legal ownership of the disputed strip, but it does not automatically mean that the paving must be demolished. The Moore-Elphicks had previously threatened to cut through the paved section running across their land. Following the tribunal’s ruling, the future use of that portion of the driveway remains uncertain.Connor, who advised on the Channel Tunnel project, and Pasquire will have to contend with the outcome of the ownership dispute, while the neighbouring couple have succeeded in defending their claim to the land. The case highlights how seemingly minor boundary disagreements can develop into lengthy legal battles, particularly when changes to a property’s access involve land belonging to someone else.You use AI every day. articles.title: French far-right author Zemmour launches second bid for 2027 presidency
articles.summary: Zemmour seeks to expel ‘foreign unemployed people’ after last month’s violent protests.
articles.body:
French far-right Eric Zemmour, known for his anti-Islam and anti-immigrant stance, says he’ll be standing in next year’s presidential election.

“I can confirm to you that I will indeed be ⁠a candidate in the presidential election”, Zemmour told TF1 TV, adding that he was running to “keep a France that is French”.

Zemmour, a 68-year-old Jewish author and veteran television commentator, finished fourth in the 2022 presidential election.

This time, he says he wants to expel foreign offenders who are in prison, as well as “foreign unemployed people who have been out of work for more than six months”, even if they are legal residents.

He says he wants “two million fewer immigrants” in France, who are seen by many among the far right as key instigators of violence during last month’s student-led cost of living protests.

Last month’s violence has led to the soaring popularity of frontrunner Marine Le Pen, with whom Zemmour will be competing against in April 2027.

Le Pen, who is the leader of the far-right National Rally party, is widely projected to win the election to replace Emmanuel Macron, who will end his term as president of France.

Meanwhile, far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon of the France Unbowed party, who has been accused of encouraging the unrest, unveiled his programme on Saturday to some 17,000 supporters.

articles.title: Fire contained on platform in Iran’s South Pars gas field
articles.summary: Officials are considering a gas leak or an operational mishap as possible causes of the fire, Fars news agency said.
articles.body:
Iranian authorities have contained a fire that broke out on a platform in South Pars gas field, the world’s largest offshore natural gas field.

The Pars Oil and Gas Company said the fire broke out on Tuesday on a gas platform in Phase 14 of the South Pars field and was extinguished immediately, Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency reported.

“During the incident, 17 workers jumped into the sea to save their lives; rescue operations for them are currently underway,” Kourosh Dehghan, Bushehr Province’s director general of crisis management, told Fars.

“Further details regarding the scale of the incident and the condition of the workers will be announced later,” Dehghan added.

Bushehr’s crisis management office later said all 17 workers were in good condition after boarding lifeboats and rescue craft, and that three heavy rescue vessels had been sent to the platform to bring them back.

Officials are considering a gas leak or an operational mishap as possible causes for the fire, Fars said.

The news agency added that the platform accounts for only 14.5 million cubic metres of South Pars’s total daily production of more than 700 million cubic metres of gas.

Iran shares the reservoir with major gas exporter Qatar, which calls its portion the North Dome.

The reservoir contains an estimated 1,800 trillion cubic feet (51 trillion cubic metres) of usable gas, enough to supply the world’s needs for 13 years.

articles.title: Poundland hopeful for last-minute rescue deal to stave off collapse
articles.summary: The BBC understands the discount chain, which has been edging towards administration, will be given more time to find a buyer.
articles.body:
Poundland and its 11,000 employees are hopeful that the retailer's impending collapse can be delayed to allow time for a last-minute rescue deal.

The discount chain has been edging towards administration after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation have told the BBC that they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release of £10m in funding.

A committee of MPs is set to question Gordon Brothers, Poundland's US owners, on Wednesday following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal.

Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

The investment firm has denied the claims.

But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.

However, sources close to the matter told the BBC on Tuesday that a release of £10m by its owners, while "small in the scale of things" could help at least postpone the chain's collapse while a longer term solution was explored.

The 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires on Thursday, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended.

Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners.

Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget.

He added the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where there were losses of £68m.

However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland stores which could mean continuing employment for workers in the event the chain is broken up and sold off in chunks.

The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain.

articles.title: Antidepressant escitalopram more effective at preventing relapse, analysis finds
articles.summary: Three pills came top and outperformed Prozac for preventing relapse in a large number of patients.
articles.body:
One drug comes out top in a large analysis of how effective antidepressants are at keeping patients free of symptoms of depression.

Escitalopram performed best at preventing patients from relapsing in a study involving nearly 10,000 people prescribed different medications for up to a year.

Two other pills - agomelatine and duloxetine - came next, while prozac (also known as fluoxetine) ranked just below them.

Experts stress the findings don't mean that everyone with severe depression should switch to escitalopram, or that other antidepressants aren't any good, because all the drugs can work and each has its pros and cons.

Depression is common, affecting around one in six people in the UK. With the right treatment and support, people can make a good recovery although for some their depression can return.

To prevent relapse, doctors already recommend people stay on antidepressants for at least six months after depression ends, and then taper off gradually.

The new analysis, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, looked at previous studies comparing the effectiveness of more than a dozen common antidepressants in total.

The differences found were modest and experts say longer studies are still needed to find out more.

There are many contributing causes to depression and a variety of ways to treat it, including drugs and talking therapies. Experts say patients should discuss what treatment options are best with their doctor.

What is escitalopram and how does it work?

Many medical guidelines recommend SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) antidepressants, like escitalopram, sertraline and fluoxetine or Prozac, as the first drug of choice.

These drugs increase seratonin, which is linked to mood.

According to the new analysis, compared to Prozac (fluoxetine):

people on escitalopram were more likely to see their symptoms improve and stay that way, and less likely to stop taking their medication

agomelatine (an atypical antidepressant) and duloxetine (an SNRI or selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor) also performed well

other medicines, including sertraline, were no better

One of the researchers, Prof Eric Ruhé at Radboud University in The Netherlands, said the choice of medication can vary for each individual.

"Nevertheless, our study can help inform the decisions that prescribers and patients make together: if you start an antidepressant, choose one that not only helps you to get well, but also keeps you well."

Dr Sameer Jauhar, an expert at Imperial College London, said while the research provided useful information, "it cannot tell us which antidepressant will work best for an individual patient."

"I would not interpret these findings as a reason for someone who is responding well to their current antidepressant to change treatment," he added.

Prof Allan Young from the Royal College of Psychiatrists said: "While some medicines appear to have a small advantage over others for longer-term outcomes, the differences are modest and are unlikely to outweigh individual factors such as side effects, previous response and patient preference when deciding on treatment."

Like all medicines, escitalopram can cause side effects, including sleep problems, constipation and weight gain, although not everyone experiences them.

The NHS says if escitalopram or a similar SSRI is ineffective or not suitable, doctors may suggest a different type of antidepressant, such as an SNRI.

Older tricyclic antidepressants, such amitriptyline, are now less commonly prescribed.

The mental health charity Mind says people need access to clear information about the potential benefits and side effects of antidepressants as well as other forms of support, including talking therapies and mindfulness.

"It's common for people to need to try more than one medication before they find the right treatment that works for them. And what works may change over time," the charity said.

Mind's website has information to help compare different antidepressants.

articles.title: El Niño in Kenya: 'It can kill us,' says Nairobi resident
articles.summary: Forecasters warn that this year's El Niño could be one of the strongest on record, with heavy rain and flooding in Kenya.
articles.body:
"It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the six-foot [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya.

Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi.

The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water.

Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives.

"Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it."

With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid – especially following warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding.

"I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us."

Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the frontline of preparations for the potential impact of El Niño.

Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world.

In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual.

Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water.

This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El Niño .

Similar work to unclog drainage systems is ongoing across Nairobi, a sprawling city built on hilly ground crossed by three major rivers.

But the workers have a huge task on their hands.

Blocked drains and inadequate sewage systems were widely blamed for the high number of deaths after the floods earlier in the year, as the excess rainfall had nowhere to escape.

The Nairobi County disaster management chief, Bramwell Simiyu tells the BBC that drainage systems have been "untouched for many years" and that removing the rubbish from them will save lives.

Floods disproportionately affect informal settlements in Nairobi, especially those near rivers, like Kibera and Mathare.

In most of these settlements, houses sit just a few metres from rivers. Some people, including Shikoli, live on the slopes of the river itself due to the constant expansion of the settlements. When flash floods occur, these houses are swept away, endangering the lives of their occupants.

Nairobi's drainage system hasn't been upgraded to deal with the rapid growth in the population and infrastructure over the decades

"The existing drainage system was developed 30 years ago to cater for a population of about 2.5 million residents but we're dealing with about 7 million in the daytime and 5.5 million night-time," Simiyu says.

He adds that investment of up to $192m (£143m) is needed to upgrade the sewerage and drainage system entirely.

But there is little sign that either the cash-strapped national or city council will able to raise this kind of money.

The Nairobi River Basin Regeneration programme, a government programme aimed at restoring the city's rivers, found that settlements near rivers, and where there is weak enforcement of regulations, have increased flooding risks. It recommended a "buffer" to protect rivers and "humane relocation" of communities where necessary.

However, rising poverty has driven many people to live close to rivers.

"Our worst case scenario looking at low-income settlements is that up to about 100,000 people are at risk," Simiyu says. "Moderate projections is about 5,000 households or about 20,000 people may be at risk."

Anyone forced to leave their homes will be relocated to 167 designated holding grounds where a stockpile of relief food and supplies will be distributed, Simiyu says.

Nobody knows exactly when the rains will come – or how much rain there will be.

But Kenya's meteorological department warns that November is usually the peak rainfall month of the short rainy season, which normally lasts from October to December.

A regional forecast from the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (Igad) warned in September that there was "an 81% probability of a very strong El Niño during October–December 2026".

So far, the heavy rains predicted have not occurred but experts remain concerned.

In East Africa, this El Niño is being widely compared to a similar weather event in 1997-1998 which caused widespread flooding and destruction in Somalia and Kenya.

Weather forecaster Jemima Gacheru tells the BBC that's because temperature conditions in the Indian Ocean in the 1997 El Niño and those recorded now are similar. This interaction, she says, has been seen to result in very strong rainfall.

"For this season we have a very strong El Niño already in play in the Pacific and then we have a positive Indian Ocean dipole," Gacheru said. This is often called the "Indian Niño" because of its similarity to its Pacific equivalent and refers to the difference in sea-surface temperatures in opposite parts of the Indian Ocean .

"We expect to have some enhanced rainfall over several parts of the country."

The UN's migration body the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that almost 900,000 people could be forced to leave their homes in Kenya this year, mostly because of the predicted floods.

Kenya is not the only African country worried about the potential impact of El Niño.

In neighbouring Somalia, the country's disaster management agency has warned that 1.2 million people are at risk of displacement caused by extreme weather – including the risk of both floods and drought.

The 1998 floods killed 2,000 people in Somalia and forced a further 250,000 to flee their homes, according to the Food and Agriculture Organisation. Up to 80% of crops were destroyed in some parts of the country.

The United Nation's famine warning system IPC has warned of the increased risk of food insecurity in Somalia due to supply chain issues exacerbated by the impact of El Niño.

Elsewhere on the continent forecasters fear El Niño could bring extreme heat and prolonged periods without rain.

It could cause a crisis for farmers across parts of West Africa, including the semi-arid Sahel region south of the Sahara, as well as in southern parts of the continent, where the risk of crop failure is high.

There are fears El Niño's impact will worsen existing issues.

Communities like Kibera are already grappling with poor housing and rampant poverty, while parts of Somalia are already in the middle of a devastating drought.

National governments in many countries are doing what they can to prepare but the extent of El Niño's impact is impossible to predict.

Back in Kibera, Shikoli and her family are preparing for the worst.

Council officials have told them they should leave their home on the riverbank until the rainy season has passed but Shikoli makes just $2 (£1.5) a day selling groundnuts and fruit from a small stall next to the river.

"I want to move," she says. "But I don't have the means.

"We just have to persevere and leave it to God."

articles.title: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting
articles.summary: The conflict in the Gulf is an opportunity for the US to test its autonomous mine-hunting systems.
articles.body:
Traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most dangerous trips a vessel can take.

Despite assistance from the US Navy, ships are still being attacked .

"To transit the Strait of Hormuz you need agreement between the captain and the crew to take the risk. You need war risk insurance. And the captain has to make the final decision," says Steve Cameron, a former merchant navy officer and maritime consultant.

Missiles and drones are a threat from the air, but under the surface mines may also be lurking.

"If you're a captain, you'd like to see evidence mines aren't present," Cameron adds.

Modern mines rest on the seabed and detonate when they detect an acoustic or magnetic signal, triggering a pressure wave that will break the keel of a passing vessel.

Others can rise through shallow waters or float, or be powered towards a target.

The technology itself is not difficult or costly, but the mere threat can stop a tanker fleet from sailing.

Ian McFarlane of French defence group Thales is a naval architect who knows mine warfare well. "Mines are a very cheap way of waging a naval war, as the Royal Navy is acutely aware," he says.

Finding sea mines has traditionally been the job of specialist mine-hunting vessels, with crews of around 80 sailors.

To keep humans out of harm's way, an increasing amount of the work is done by systems that are autonomous and monitored from the shore.

They might only need 20 personnel, working in shifts on land. With the recruitment and retention challenges facing Nato navies these highly-portable robot systems are very attractive.

Such tech has been under development for 20 years.

During the 2003 Iraq war the US Navy poked around the seabed looking for mines with a torpedo-shaped robot called the Remus 100.

Pinging around with sonar these little machines operated down to around 100ft depth and spared divers a difficult and dangerous task.

The latest conflict in the Gulf is testing much more capable systems.

The US military is sparing with details about their mine-hunting craft, but we have seen glimpses of them.

Iranian forces hauled an uncrewed US autonomous sub out of the waters of the Strait of Hormuz in early September.

The Pentagon claimed this robot, an Extra Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) from US autonomous defence tech venture Anduril, was a malfunctioning older device with no classified equipment on-board.

Whatever its mission, no sailors were imperilled. That, says William Lupton, a naval analyst with Shephard Group, "was a drop in the ocean compared to having prisoners taken", and part of the point of uncrewed vessels.

What if an uncrewed vessel is captured? Nato navies are reluctant to go into details, but computer drives can be wiped or destroyed remotely by various means. This may have taken place inside the humming circuit boards of the XLUUV seized by Iran.

Such autonomous tech is being embraced by forces around the world.

Cooperation between Thales, the Royal Navy, and France's Marine Nationale has produced a robot motor launch.

The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle (USV) is packed with sensors programmed to detect mines via sonar that was developed for the oil and gas industries.

It tows a 5m long rectangular box, similar to a large torpedo, that takes a hi-resolution look at the seabed and creates a 3D picture refined by AI. The latest mines are designed to blend into their surroundings and the software spots anything that looks like a mine.

Autonomous systems are cheaper than conventional minehunters, plus they can be deployed, along with containerised control centres, by air.

Steve Prest, associate fellow at the RUSI defence think tank, introduced uncrewed mine hunting into the Royal Navy and was its first fleet robotics officer, a title he acquired in 2014.

"There is a bunch of ways to look for a mine using robot boats or robot subs, and while you can't prove the negative, that no mines are there, you can reduce the risk."

He says US robot minehunters can either blow up a mine or just mark the spot as somewhere to avoid.

"We'll see more use of autonomy but also the missions and capability will expand. And AI will be analysing data from those vessels on the spot as opposed to data being analysed when a drone returns."

The Royal Navy recently announced its concept of a hybrid navy - mixing drones with conventional warships. But Prest thinks for this vision to succeed the fleet must operate as one distributed force, sharing data in what he terms a cognitive architecture.

The robot only makes a real difference as part of this scheme and it's a mistake to focus on individual uncrewed assets. "Uncrewed or autonomous vessels are not the operating system. They are applications running on it."

While robots are on the rise, people are what really matter in the Strait.

Neil Roberts speaks for insurers at Lloyd's of London on marine matters and says the psychological impact of the mine threat is inescapable, as is the uncertainty around just how many mines, if any, are out there.

"The US says it has cleared the Omani route and believes the mine threat is being managed, with shipments running at about 75% of pre-conflict levels."

Fear of the unknown is the most potent aspect of the sea mine threat and robots are now the weapon of choice to confront that fear.

articles.title: Sonia Gandhi: What will Congress leader's memoir reveal about India's most powerful political family?
articles.summary: Sonia Gandhi's memoir revisits love, loss and political inheritance, offering a deeply personal defence of her family and its legacy.
articles.body:
On the morning of 31 October 1984, Sonia Gandhi was a young wife and mother, living in the prime minister's residence in Delhi. She was about to take a bath when she heard shots ring out in the garden.

Her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, India's prime minister, had just left for her office in an adjoining building. Moments later, she would be assassinated by two of her Sikh bodyguards, in retaliation for the Indian army's storming of the Golden Temple in Amritsar, Sikhism's holiest shrine, earlier that year.

The sound was like firecrackers, but "different". The children's nanny came pounding on the bathroom door, hysterical, pointing towards the garden.

Sonia ran towards the path. A white Ambassador car was moving slowly towards her. Inside, Indira lay covered in blood, her sari stained, her eyes open, her face wearing what Sonia remembered as a look of surprise.

"Mummy, Mummy," she tried to say. No words came. At the hospital, she waited for hours before a doctor's shake of the head told her what she feared.

The ordeal did not end there. Rajiv Gandhi, her husband and the elder son of Indira Gandhi, summoned from a rally in West Bengal, arrived to tell her that party leaders wanted him to become prime minister.

Sonia's response was fury and terror. "They will kill you; they will kill you, too!" she pleaded. Rajiv replied: "They will kill me anyway." That evening, as Indira's body lay at home, Rajiv was sworn in.

It is one of the most searing passages in Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi's new memoir: private devastation unfolding alongside the pressures of public life.

The woman who had largely stayed away from politics was now married to India's prime minister, and would eventually find herself at the head of the Congress party, leading it through two general election victories and becoming one of the country's most consequential political figures.

The passage also foreshadows another devastating loss. In 1991, Rajiv himself was assassinated.

For Sonia, the years that followed were marked by retreat.

At 19, a young woman from a small Italian town, she had met Rajiv, an Indian student, in England. Their relationship took her into a new country and family, and a close bond with Indira followed. India became home through her husband and her mother-in-law.

After Rajiv's killing, even the public appearances required by the memorial trusts she headed became an ordeal. Before speeches, she feared tears would overwhelm her.

When the Dalai Lama asked whether she felt vengeful towards her husband's killers, she answered, "No, I don't," and burst into sobs. Slowly, she writes, Rajiv became "a presence within me rather than a piercing absence".

But grief returned at family milestones. At her son Rahul's Cambridge graduation in 1995, she and her children were overcome by the thought of how proud Rajiv would have been.

Politics, meanwhile, was closing in. The Congress party, the political vehicle of her husband's family for generations, was losing cohesion and electoral ground. Senior leaders were defecting, and the calls for Sonia to step in were growing louder.

She initially refused. She writes she had seen politics through Rajiv: its achievements, but also its "ambition and greed, hypocrisy and treachery". "I'd always disliked politics," she writes. It had taken first her mother-in-law, then "the love of my life, my children's father".

Yet the party's decline began to feel personal. Walking past photographs of Indira and Rajiv, she was seized by "a mixture of pain and guilt". She feared that the forces they had fought to "protect India's pluralistic ethos" were gaining ground: a rising Hindu nationalism that, in her view, threatened the "secular and pluralistic vision" of India they had sought to defend.

Congress leaders argued that without her, the party could splinter, leaving little to resist communal politics. The family name, she believed, carried an appeal beyond religion, caste, language and region. This, she says, was "the most compelling argument".

Her doubts were also about her own credentials. How could an outsider occupy a position held by two formidable figures? At home, Rahul and Priyanka feared losing their mother as they had lost their grandmother and father. Before a New Year holiday, they extracted a promise: "Don't you do anything crazy while we're away."

The "answer", she says, came through the Bhagavad Gita . Though not religious in adult life, Sonia arranged private lessons with a Sanskrit scholar in January 1997. They read the text verse by verse. She writes that its central message – to perform one's dharma, or duty, without attachment to the fruits of one's actions – eventually resolved her inner conflict.

"I had the answer to my own doubts and questions. I had to step out and go where my duty called. And I did."

The memoir's most dramatic political scene, however, comes seven years later, after Congress's 2004 election victory . Sonia had led the party's campaign.

Sonia goes with Manmohan Sing h to meet India's president at the presidential palace in Delhi and formally stake the Congress-led alliance's claim to form a government. Everyone assumes she will become prime minister. She says nothing.

At home, she tells a senior aide she intends to refuse. Party workers gather at the gates; senior colleagues demand a meeting.

"You fought the election, you led us," says one. "People believed in you. How can you let them down like this? Our workers will revolt. You think they'll accept another leader?"

Alliance leaders arrive to persuade her. They surround her, she recalls, and one insists: "We will not take no for an answer." Overwhelmed, she murmurs " Theek hai " - all right. They take it as consent and begin congratulating her.

Her children are appalled, she writes. Rahul storms in: "You said yes?" Her daughter Priyanka urges her not to be forced into a decision.

Sonia writes she spends a long night arguing with herself, friends and family. The risk is not merely personal. She believes the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) would continue to exploit her foreign birth and that accepting office would allow the controversy to "create havoc" and hurt the country. By morning she is clear. " I've made up my mind . I'm going to stick to my stand," she tells Rahul.

She chooses Singh, a trained economist and a party member, instead, describing him as a man "above reproach", with a "deep and consummate understanding of governance".

The book is at its most revealing when it turns from family memory to the India she believes has been lost.

Sonia says that when she entered public life there was "a certain decency and decorum in parliamentary politics".

Political attacks and harsh words were not new, but she sees a sharper appetite among those in power "to belittle and torment those who differ from them, to intimidate those they perceive as opponents". It is, she says, part of a wider international drift towards "a heartlessness that accompanies authoritarian regimes".

Her portrait of prime minister Narendra Modi of the Hindu nationalist BJP is unusually direct.

The two have had "practically no real contact", she writes, beyond formal greetings at parliamentary gatherings and occasional exchanges - " Theek hain, aap ?" ("Are you all right?") - when she returned from hospital. "He tends to look away," she says, "avoiding eye contact."

Modi's idea of India, she writes, was shaped by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and "affirmed a fundamentalism in which his faith and culture superseded all others". His is an India of "hierarchy, order, and control"; hers is "an India against hegemony", standing for "inclusiveness, secularism, and social justice".

There is a striking concession amid the polemic - she says she understood Modi's "discomfort with the ruling elite of our times".

Sonia says she felt uneasy in Delhi's privileged drawing rooms, where political conversation seemed "very far removed from the reality of India".

Modi's origins, she writes, "may not be as humble as his PR team" suggests, but he "had certainly worked his way to power within the RSS from an underprivileged world". It is a rare acknowledgement of the social distance between the Congress establishment and the electorate Modi came to represent.

The memoir also offers some glimpses of Sonia's encounters with world leaders.

She remembers Vladimir Putin as an "engaging personality" who took her on a boat ride in St Petersburg, pointing out monuments along the way. She says she was impressed by his grasp of geopolitics and his "determination to restore Russia to its former powerful status" - "long before the Ukraine war, a different era".

A more amusing encounter involved France's Nicolas Sarkozy, who arrived in India in 2008 without his then partner Carla Bruni because they were unmarried.

At a state banquet, the Indian vice-president's wife cheerfully grilled him about when he planned to marry her, whether he missed her and whether a date had been fixed. Sarkozy obligingly answered her questions while messaging Bruni on his phone.

Belonging is not a neutral history. The Bofors gun scandal, which badly damaged Rajiv Gandhi's government and dogged the family for decades, gets a relatively brief treatment.

The 502-page memoir is less forthcoming about the less flattering aspects of Congress's own record. Sonia has much to say about political corruption, hypocrisy and the decline of public standards under her opponents, but largely sidesteps the culture of patronage, cronyism and corruption that dogged Congress during its years in power. There is little reckoning, either, with the party's own share of responsibility for the erosion of public trust.

She is at pains to defend the political inheritance of her husband and mother-in-law, even as the party they built has suffered a prolonged decline. The story she tells is as much about the costs of carrying that inheritance as it is about a woman who says she never wanted the life she ended up leading.

That gives the memoir's final pages an unmistakable melancholy. Sonia, 79, is now a member of the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of parliament. Rahul, 55, is a four-term MP and leader of the opposition; Priyanka, 53, is also a member of parliament.

Sonia says the challenge was to remain faithful to "a just and humane society", through pain and loss, victory and defeat, and the manoeuvring that politics demands. But she ends not with triumph, nor even with the assurance that history will vindicate her.

"At this moment it seems to me that, although I tried my best, I didn't succeed in beating back the forces I'd set out to fight."

articles.title: Duchy tenants may have to buy farms or leave as Prince William plans sell-off
articles.summary: A ten-year strategy to raise £500m from the Duchy of Cornwall will see farms sold off across England.
articles.body:
Plans by the Prince of Wales to sell off up to 20% of the Duchy of Cornwall could see more tenant farmers across England asked to buy their farms or move out.

Up to 40 farm holdings across Devon, Cornwall, Herefordshire and the Midlands could be affected by the sale, according to the Tenant Farmers Association (TFA).

Locals say talks over the future of nine farms on the Bradninch estate in Devon have already caused "distress" for some tenants who fear they cannot afford to buy.

A spokeswoman said the Duchy could not confirm the total number of tenants affected by the ten-year sale plan but told the BBC the estate was "supporting them through the process with care and respect".

The Duchy, which covers around 51,800 hectares (128,000 acres) in 19 counties, plans to use the £500m raised from the property and land sale over the next decade to invest in local communities, affordable housing and environmental projects.

Former GP Mary Ryan, a local Lib Dem councillor who has lived near the Bradninch estate for around 35 years and is supporting the farmers, said some of those affected were "experiencing enormous mental and emotional distress" as a result of the planned sell-off.

She added that while the Duchy had reportedly apologised to tenants last month, the handling of the process had been "pretty dire".

The sales programme has now been extended from Bradninch, near Cullompton, to the Duloe Estate in Cornwall and to individual holdings elsewhere in Cornwall, Herefordshire and the Midlands, according to the TFA.

The Duchy's rural director, Matthew Morris, told the BBC he was listening to feedback over how the sales were being handled and offering support and mental health advice to tenants.

Morris added that the Duchy was "still committed to agriculture" but that there "may well be other disposals in the future".

In terms of immediate evictions, he said, there were "no cliff edges here" and that the Duchy was working closely with every tenant to find a suitable outcome.

"In the main, our mission is to sell to our farmers. We are keen that wherever possible we can achieve that continuity," Morris explained.

"For many of our farmers, it's a generational aspiration to own their farm. A few people have said it to me: 'My grandfather wanted to buy his farm. My father wanted to buy the farm. And now I've got the opportunity and it's an amazing outcome'.

"That's kind of what's driving me through what, at times, has been a little bit of turbulence."

The Duchy - which was established in 1337 - currently has around 700 agricultural lettings, with around 300 whole farm holdings made up of a farmhouse, land and buildings.

Farmers are on a mix of contracts ranging from time-limited to lifelong, with an option to pass the tenancy down through a family.

George Dunn, TFA chief executive, said the organisation was in "deep discussions" with the Duchy and that poor communication had led to tenants "facing prolonged uncertainty over valuations, timing and the options available to them".

"Once a family is told that its long-term relationship with the Duchy may change permanently, that uncertainty lives with them 24/7," he told the BBC.

He added that while he welcomed the Duchy's assurance that "nobody will be made homeless" not every tenant "will be able or want to buy the farms that they operate and fair alternatives must be explored for those for whom ownership is unaffordable".

A spokeswoman for the Duchy said: "We are engaging with people directly and supporting them through the process with care and respect.

"We recognise that each of our tenant's circumstances are different, and we are taking a careful, case-by-case approach."

articles.title: Prince George's art features in magazine edited by Prince William
articles.summary: The Prince of Wales features his 13-year-old son's drawing of a bird as part of a special edition of the magazine.
articles.body:
A drawing of a kingfisher by Prince George features as part of a special edition of Country Life magazine, guest edited by his father, the Prince of Wales.

The 13-year-old drew the bird, which is perched on a branch, while at home in the spring.

The artwork is included as part of a wider 300-page special edition of the magazine, in which the Princess of Wales has also given an interview.

As well as providing an insight into his family life, Prince William uses the magazine as an opportunity to shed light on the working conditions for servicewomen and feature his "fanatical" support for Aston Villa.

Prince George, who is said to enjoy drawing, appears to be following in the footsteps of his family.

His grandfather, the King, is a keen artist. Both his mother, Catherine, and uncle, the Duke of Sussex, studied art at A-level. Catherine also studied history of art at university.

Last year, Catherine, Prince George and his siblings - Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis - drew each other in four portraits posted on social media by Kensington Palace.

The palace said the royals made the sketches as "a moment of connection" to "spend time looking at and focusing on one another" while being creative.

Elsewhere in the edition, Catherine, who revealed two years ago that she was receiving cancer treatment, is said to have discussed the healing power of nature.

Prince William discusses walks with the family's dogs, Orla and Otto, and how his children love to go outside and explore. He also tells of his fondness for a pub visit and a pint of cider with ice.

Aston Villa manager Unai Emery is also featured in the magazine, and described the prince's support for the club as "fantastic" ahead of publication.

"If we can give him good news, good results or good moments in football, we are proud of it," he said in a video.

Another prominent part of the Country Life edition, published this week, is Prince William setting out his drive to ensure women in the British armed forces feel safe.

The Prince of Wales called for a military culture that is more inclusive and respectful of women, saying that more must be done to ensure women in the military are shown respect and protected from sexual harassment.

It follows the death of 19-year-old soldier Jaysley Beck in 2021. A coroner ruled the Army's failure to take action - after Gunner Beck was harassed by her line manager and sexually assaulted by another colleague - had contributed to her suicide.

Prince William is not the first senior royal to guest edit Country Life.

The King has guest edited the magazine on several occasions, including to mark his 65th and 70th birthdays. Queen Camilla and Anne, the Princess Royal , have also previously edited editions.

articles.title: US evacuates 13 military aircraft from second UK base as new Iran threat raises alarm
articles.summary: More than a dozen U.S. Air Force aircraft left RAF Mildenhall after a reported Iran-linked threat triggered the second-highest military alert level.
articles.body: The U.S. Air Force abruptly relocated more than a dozen aircraft from RAF Mildenhall in eastern England amid an emerging security threat, U.S. officials confirmed Tuesday. The Wall Street Journal first reported the move, citing sources who said the threat originated in Iran. As U.S. officials assessed the threat's nature and urgency, commanders raised the base's security level to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the military's second-highest alert level, indicating a likely terrorist threat against personnel or facilities. IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS Flight-tracking data and open-source analysts with the Military Air Tracking Alliance identified 13 U.S. aircraft leaving the base late Monday, the Associated Press said. Nine Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers were moved to airfields in Scotland, Germany and Spain. Three CV-22B Ospreys were relocated to nearby RAF Lakenheath, which has hardened aircraft shelters. A U.S. official told The Associated Press the moves were precautionary, noting that some aircraft were on rotational deployments while others were permanently stationed in the United Kingdom. IRAN UNDER SCRUTINY AFTER PLOT FOILED NEAR UK BASE USED BY US MILITARY The move marks the second major relocation of U.S. military aircraft from Britain in less than two months. In early October, the Air Force pulled heavy bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire after British counterterrorism police stopped three suspicious vans headed toward the base Sept. 27. Two men have since been charged under the United Kingdom's National Security Act. Separately, the Justice Department unsealed indictments against three Iranian-backed operatives on Tuesday accused of involvement in coordinated terrorist plots across Europe, including RAF Fairford. UK POLICE ARREST 'EXPLOSIVE' SUSPECTS NEAR US AIRBASE, KEY TO IRAN WAR RAF Mildenhall is home to the 100th Air Refueling Wing, the only permanently based U.S. tanker wing in Europe. Its KC-135 Stratotankers support allied aerial refueling and long-range strike missions across the region. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Washington routinely repositions military forces. "We are constantly repositioning forces around the world for a variety of reasons," Rubio told reporters when asked about the evacuation. articles.title: IRGC operative lands on FBI’s Most Wanted Terrorists list over alleged plot to kill former Trump advisor
articles.summary: Shahram Poursafi allegedly sought to pay $300,000 to have John Bolton killed in a plot authorities linked to retaliation for Qasem Soleimani’s death.
articles.body: The FBI on Tuesday placed a member of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on its Most Wanted Terrorists list for allegedly soliciting the murders of two former U.S. government officials. Shahram Poursafi is accused of hiring individuals to kill the officials between October 2021 and April 2022, according to the FBI’s Washington Field Office. Court documents detail an alleged plot targeting former National Security Advisor John Bolton. The assassination plot was believed to have been initiated in retaliation for the January 2020 killing of IRGC commander Qasem Soleimani, who led a unit of the Qods Force, one of the IRGC's five divisions responsible for developing and carrying out lethal plotting operations. Poursafi allegedly worked on behalf of the division and sought to pay individuals in the U.S. $300,000 to carry out the assassination. US OFFERS $20M FOR IRANIAN IN PLOT TARGETING TRUMP’S EX-NATIONAL SECURITY ADVISER JOHN BOLTON Separately, the FBI released wanted posters seeking information on three alleged IRGC officials from the same Qods Force unit. The individuals were identified as Mohammad Reza Ansari, Abolfazl Alizadeh and Mohammad Hossein Shamoradizadeh. Ansari is an alleged deputy who has supported IRGC operations in Syria. He also allegedly planned and attempted to assassinate two former U.S. government officials with the Poursafi’s support. Alizadeh and Shamoradizadeh are both alleged battalion commanders who have participated in lethal plotting operations. articles.title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
articles.summary: The US Department of Justice says the men were involved in a string of plots, including a major incident near the UK airbase that is used by US armed forces.
articles.body:
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.

The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.

One man, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of doing the same from Iran.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford incident, which came to light when suspicious vans were reported near the base. Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident.

Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.

It accuses the trio of planning attacks in Europe that were carried out under the name of a purportedly new group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand - HAYI).

"Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK," the DOJ statement said. It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".

Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year.

"This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.

He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.

Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.

A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase.

No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.

The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot".

On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said.

In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged.

According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel".

The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated.

"On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base."

The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive.

"At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added.

It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police.

What we know about RAF Fairford counter-terror probe

The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot.

The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason.

RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

articles.title: New photos 'essential evidence' of possible SAS war crimes, inquiry hears
articles.summary: The inquiry's lead barrister says photos of people lying on their backs with shots to the head may be evidence of possible war crimes.
articles.body:
An inquiry into UK special forces operations in Afghanistan has released photos described as "essential evidence", showing soldiers could have executed unarmed people laying asleep.

For the first time, the inquiry has made public photos taken of the deceased, across two SAS operations, that show multiple individuals lying in bed with shots to the head.

The inquiry's lead barrister, Oliver Glasgow KC, said the photos may be evidence of possible war crimes and worthy of expert interrogation.

The public inquiry is examining allegations that the SAS murdered unarmed civilians and detainees on night raids between 2010 and 2013 and planted weapons to cover up the killings.

The graphic photographs show multiple unarmed people lying in bed.

One person was tucked under a floral blanket, others with their heads on pillows, blood pooling around their heads. Blood spatter is visible low on the wall in one of the images, consistent with someone being shot while lying down.

Glasgow described how many "look like they sustained head shots" and in a number of cases "there appears to be a dead body with his head on a pillow".

He said further analysis may be able to confirm if the people in the photographs were "shot when asleep".

Seventeen people were killed across the two operations which took place in Helmand province in 2011. The youngest of those killed in each of the operations were 15 and 14 years old respectively.

Glasgow said the photos appeared to contradict the accounts given by the SAS and would have raised serious questions for the military police officers investigating the operations as potential murders.

Lt Col John Harvey, who led the military police's murder probe, agreed they "didn't look right".

He told the inquiry his team were clear the photos could be vital evidence.

Despite the repeated requests of the police investigators to submit the photographs for further testing, this never took place.

One of the investigators, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the BBC "you can see why we were concerned", adding: "Bullet marks on the walls so low to the ground appeared to undermine the special forces' version of events."

The inquiry is subjecting the photographs to expert forensic analysis.

BBC Panorama has been investigating allegations the SAS executed unarmed civilians and children for more than eight years. The public inquiry was established in 2022 in the wake of Panorama's revelations.

The photos appear to support the findings of Panorama's 2022 investigation into raids in Helmand province which took place a decade before.

Panorama travelled to Afghanistan to gather evidence related to four raids on homes that killed 26 people.

The BBC visited the same guesthouses where the photographs released by the inquiry on Tuesday were taken. Panorama's team were the first British investigators to visit the sites of the shootings, despite a five-year-long military police investigation.

Official special forces accounts of the incidents claim Taliban insurgents opened fire on troops as they entered the compounds, forcing the SAS to return fire and kill those inside.

However weaponry experts told the BBC evidence collected by Panorama indicated multiple rounds appeared to have been fired from above.

This suggests those killed were either lying down or sitting against the wall and not in a firefight.

Family members also told Panorama those killed had been shot cleanly in the head or chest - a common characteristic of a deliberate SAS shooting at close range.

The photographs released by the inquiry show multiple "traumatic injuries to the head or face" of those killed by the SAS, according to its lead barrister.

The inquiry also heard evidence that calls into question whether alleged war crimes were thoroughly investigated.

It heard how investigators were still in Afghanistan in July 2019 gathering evidence as senior officers prepared to close their murder investigation and inform ministers.

The military police investigators were looking for eyewitnesses to unlawful killings and the planting of weapons.

One member of the Afghan partner unit that served on operations alongside the SAS told military police he had personally witnessed a British soldier planting a rifle on an unarmed person after they had been killed.

articles.title: US army officer arrested in UK on suspicion of spying for Russia
articles.summary: A US army officer assigned to a Nato unit in UK was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion of espionage linked to Russia, British counterterrorism police and
articles.body: A US army officer assigned to a Nato unit in UK was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion of espionage linked to Russia, British counterterrorism police and other officials said.The arrest comes amid growing concerns over threats to American forces stationed in Britain and heightened tensions between Moscow and much of Europe.The 41-year-old man, whose identity has not been disclosed, was arrested near Gloucester under two provisions of the National Security Act 2023 -- assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information.The suspect was serving with Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester, according to a US official, a senior Nato official and a British government official. The US official said the man was an officer. All three spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.The Allied Rapid Reaction Corps is a multinational land unit within Nato designed to respond swiftly to crises and short-notice operations. According to its website, the formation comprises forces from 20 nations but is led by Britain and based in Gloucester, where the US soldier was arrested.US Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, commanding general of the army's Counterintelligence Command, described the suspect as a senior soldier in a news release but provided no further details about his identity. Authorities have not disclosed additional information about the case.The metropolitan police said its counterterrorism officers worked closely with the FBI and the US military. FBI director Kash Patel described the arrest as an “important arrest" involving espionage allegations that are of “utmost concern” for the US and its allies.“This FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners," Patel said.The suspect was being held at a London police station, officials said. Searches were carried out at two locations in Gloucestershire, a county about 140 kilometres west of London.Police said the arrest was unrelated to other counterterrorism investigations, ruling out a connection with a suspected terror plot linked to Iran in September at RAF Fairford, a US-run airbase near Gloucester.Following that threat, the US air force withdrew bombers that had been used to strike Iran from RAF Fairford. The air force also relocated aircraft from another British base, RAF Mildenhall, earlier this week following a threat that The Wall Street Journal reported was linked to Iran.Tuesday's arrest near Gloucester appears to be separate from those incidents, with authorities indicating that the investigation concerns Russia.Several European countries have recently warned of an escalating threat from Russian covert operations, including sabotage, espionage and drone incursions.Denmark's defence intelligence service said Russian President Vladimir Putin could launch military attacks against Nato only if he believed the alliance would not respond collectively and “especially if Russia assesses that the United States cannot or will not support the European Nato countries in a potential war against Russia.”Nato's supreme allied commander, US General Alexus Grynkewich, said last month that the alliance was prepared to fight if attacked. He made the remarks in Poland while outlining Nato's plans to defend against a possible Russian attack.Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the news agency AP has tracked more than 210 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe attributed to Russia by Western officials. These include alleged plots to set fire to warehouses, drone launches, attempts to kill enemies abroad, theft of defence technology and cyberattacks targeting critical European infrastructure.One of the latest incidents was an attempted drone attack on a German airport in August that officials blamed on Russia. The incident prompted Germany to shut down a Russian consulate.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Unfit to remain in office’: Eisenkot attacks Netanyahu after ‘hateful’ Knesset speech
articles.summary: Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has cancelled a scheduled meeting with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party to discuss coalition negotiations,
articles.body: Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has cancelled a scheduled meeting with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party to discuss coalition negotiations, after the Israeli prime minister delivered a speech at the swearing-in of the new Knesset that Eisenkot described as “delusional, divisive, hateful and disgraceful”.The cancellation came a day after Netanyahu called on opposition leaders to join a national unity government, arguing that Israel needed a united front in the face of the Iranian nuclear threat.In his address to parliament on Tuesday, he renewed that appeal but also criticised opposition leaders for considering a government supported by Arab-majority parties.Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming Israel’s next government, said Netanyahu’s remarks had reinforced his belief that the outgoing prime minister was unfit to remain in office.“I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister’s delusional, divisive, hateful and disgraceful speech, in which he abused a state occasion at the swearing-in of the 26th Knesset. I became even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute,” Eisenkot wrote on X.“We must act urgently to establish a national emergency government. His continued rule is dividing Israel and endangering its security,” he added, calling on opposition leaders Yair Lapid, Yair Golan, Avigdor Liberman and Naftali Bennett to take responsibility.Yashar cancels meeting with LikudYashar had earlier announced that its negotiating team was due to meet Likud representatives on Wednesday as part of efforts to form the next government.“Following Yashar's appeal to all Knesset factions to conduct sincere and genuine negotiations based on the four principles set out by Yashar for forming a government, a negotiation meeting was scheduled for tomorrow between the Eisenkot team and Likud,” the party said in a statement, according to The Jerusalem Post.However, it said Eisenkot had instructed his team to cancel the meeting following Netanyahu’s speech and conduct during the Knesset swearing-in ceremony.The party accused Netanyahu of choosing political survival over national unity, saying his address was another indication that he did not want to bring Israelis together.“As always, when faced with a choice between the gravity of the moment and the resilience of Israeli society on one hand, and his political survival on the other, Netanyahu will always choose himself. At any cost,” the statement said.Netanyahu attacks possible coalition with Arab partiesNetanyahu, meanwhile, has continued to push for a unity government, saying opposition parties should set aside their differences in view of the security challenges facing Israel.During his speech, he questioned whether Jewish opposition leaders were prepared to depend on Arab politicians to form a government.“I ask you: Are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?” he said, according to news agency AP.He also took to X to criticise the possibility of a government supported by Ra’am and the Joint List, calling the proposed arrangement “dangerous”.“Shame! It is forbidden to form a dangerous government with the terror supporters of Ra’am and the Joint List!” Netanyahu wrote.The Likud party also criticised Yashar’s decision to cancel the meeting. It said Netanyahu would “turn over every stone to achieve national unity” and remained willing to meet representatives of any faction seeking unity.Likud described the cancellation as “puzzling”, arguing that Eisenkot and other opposition parties were continuing negotiations with Arab parties even as they called off talks with Netanyahu’s party.The criticism followed the departure of Arab lawmakers during the national anthem at the Knesset swearing-in ceremony, as reported by The Jerusalem Post.Eisenkot seeks to form government as new Knesset begins workThe dispute comes as Eisenkot works to assemble a coalition after receiving the mandate to form Israel’s next government from President Isaac Herzog. His bloc secured recommendations from representatives of 67 lawmakers, including support from Ra’am and the Joint List.The election left the 120-member Knesset without a clear majority. Netanyahu’s Likud-led faction secured 53 seats, while Eisenkot’s Yashar alliance won 48. A government needs the support of at least 61 lawmakers to command a majority.Eisenkot has up to six weeks to form a government that would end Netanyahu’s tenure as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. If he fails, Herzog is expected to give Netanyahu another opportunity to form an administration.Meanwhile, Eisenkot’s bloc has begun advancing its legislative agenda in the new parliament. It has introduced bills seeking a government-led inquiry into Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attacks, term limits for the prime minister and the reversal of changes made by Netanyahu’s outgoing government to limit the judiciary’s powers.The opposition has also initiated the process to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, who is backed by Netanyahu. It has nominated Matan Kahana, a senior member of Yashar, for the position.Netanyahu and his Cabinet remain in office during the transition, even as the newly sworn-in Knesset begins legislative work.As caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu retains authority over national security and the military, while facing court-imposed limits on some of his powers.You use AI every day. articles.title: US charges 3 ‘Iranian-backed’ men over alleged plot at UK Fairford air base
articles.summary: The men, including one who is already in jail, face charges over alleged plot at UK air base used in US war on Iran.
articles.body:
Prosecutors in the United States have charged three men they describe as Iranian-backed operatives over their alleged role in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across the US and Europe, including a plot targeting the United Kingdom’s Fairford air base .

The Department of Justice said on Tuesday that the three men acted in support of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Iraq’s Kataib Hezbollah.

It identified the men as Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, who face what it called “terrorism-related offenses”.

Al-Saadi is already in jail in New York. Prosecutors did not disclose the whereabouts of Mohajeri and al-Hassani.

The charges announced on Tuesday centre on RAF Fairford in southwest England, where US forces and bombers had been stationed. The US had used the base to deploy bombers in its war against Iran.

Police were called to the Fairford site in September after a local farmer reported seeing a group of men with several white vans engaged in “suspicious” activity.

Six men were arrested in connection with the episode, and all were released on bail. Two were subsequently re-arrested on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service and charged under the National Security Act.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the incident.

Days after the incident, the US withdrew all of its B-1 bombers from Fairford.

A US charging document said that al-Hassani, a 35-year-old Iraqi national, directed others to drive to the base in the vans, some of which carried barrels of fuel. Prosecutors say he had earlier paid the group to buy metal objects that could serve as shrapnel and to disguise the vans as fuel delivery vehicles.

Prosecutors said al-Saadi, 32, who holds Iranian and Iraqi citizenship, passed coded messages to al-Hassani and Mohajeri, a 48-year-old Iranian, to coordinate the plot.

Al-Saadi did so, they said, in phone calls to his mother and sister in Iraq, using coded language.

“These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said Manhattan US Attorney Jamie McDonald.

“The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical – it is very real.”

There was no immediate comment from Iran on the charges.

US authorities first detailed the charges against al-Saadi in May, accusing him of directing others to attack US, Israeli and Jewish targets and to kill Americans, in retaliation for the US-Israel war on Iran.

Those attacks included the nonfatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London in April and arson attacks on synagogues, Israeli businesses and Jewish schools elsewhere in Europe.

Al-Saadi has been in US custody since May.

In June, he pleaded not guilty to those charges and called himself a “prisoner of war”. He has been held without bail since his arrest.

The indictment on Tuesday added his alleged role in the Fairford plot and charges the other two men.

Flight-tracking data showed on Tuesday that the US military had removed at least a dozen aircraft from a second UK airbase, RAF Mildenhall, following what the Wall Street Journal said was a threat from Iran.
